title: Beeck v. Aquaslide 'N' Dive Corp.
lead: A water-slide manufacturer withdrew its admission of manufacture after the injury limitations period expired, and a separate trial resolved the disputed product identity.

actors.name: Jerry and Judy Beeck
actors.role: Injured user and spouse seeking damages

actors.name: Carl Meyer
actors.role: Aquaslide president who later inspected the slide

proceedings: District court allowed an amended denial of manufacture and a separate identity trial.
Jury found for Aquaslide; district court dismissed by summary judgment.
Eighth Circuit affirmed both discretionary rulings.
limits: The identity verdict was not challenged on appeal. Potential claims against others were uncertain, not guaranteed. Review of amendment used the record when leave was granted, not the subsequent verdict.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: An apparently branded slide causes severe injury
sections.cue: Several investigations agree on the manufacturer
paragraphs: In 1971 Kimberly Village in Davenport, Iowa, ordered an Aquaslide through distributor George Boldt. The order passed through Sentry Pool and Chemical Supply to Purity Swimming Pool Supply, whose warehouse delivered the slide. Kimberly employees installed it. It resembled an Aquaslide but lacked identifying marks, and Kimberly believed it was the ordered product.

On July 15, 1972, Jerry Beeck was severely injured while using that slide at a gathering sponsored by his employer, Harker Wholesale Meats. He and his wife Judy sued Aquaslide alone, alleging it manufactured the slide and seeking a combined $2,225,000 for negligence, strict liability, and implied warranty.

Investigators for Beeck’s employer’s insurer, Kimberly’s insurer, and Aquaslide’s insurer all identified Aquaslide as the manufacturer. The company learned of the accident in October 1972, and its insurer inspected in May 1973. With those investigations and no contrary information, Aquaslide admitted manufacture in its December 12, 1973 answer and June 3, 1974 interrogatory responses.

sections.title: A later inspection changes the defense
sections.cue: The amendment follows expiration of limitations
paragraphs: Iowa’s two-year personal-injury limitations period expired July 15, 1974. About six and a half months later, Aquaslide president and owner Carl Meyer inspected before his deposition, apparently at plaintiffs’ request to investigate installation or assembly defects. He concluded that Aquaslide had not made the slide. The company sought permission to amend its answer; the Beecks continued to dispute its new position.

District Judge Hanson permitted the amendment over the Beecks' objection and granted Aquaslide's request for a separate jury trial on whether Aquaslide designed, manufactured, or sold the slide. The jury found for Aquaslide, and the court entered summary judgment dismissing the action. The Beecks appealed permission to amend and separation of the trial, but did not challenge the jury’s nonmanufacture finding.

sections.title: The appellate court examines the amendment when it was allowed
sections.cue: Possible prejudice does not compel a binding false admission
paragraphs: District Judge Paul Benson, sitting with Circuit Judges Bright and Henley, applied abuse-of-discretion review. Rule 15(a) favored leave when justice required, subject to reasons including undue delay, bad faith, dilatory motive, repeated failed amendments, prejudice, and futility. Opponents bore the burden of showing prejudice in the circumstances.

The district court had evaluated good faith, diligence, and prejudice. Aquaslide relied on three insurers’ investigations, and nobody claimed it manipulated their result. Responsibility for the mistaken identification was shared, and investigative shortcomings did not require forfeiting the identity defense. The court did not pronounce the investigation perfect.

To treat the expired limitations period as necessarily fatal when amendment was requested would require assuming both that Aquaslide would prevail on identity and that every other possible action was barred. Neither was established then. Possible substitution in the distribution chain might support fraud or contract claims with other limitations periods, or equitable estoppel might affect another defendant’s defense. The appellate court neither found a substitution nor guaranteed another remedy. That uncertainty permitted the district court to reject speculative prejudice rather than force a company to accept liability without contesting whether it made the product.

sections.title: The identity trial avoids unnecessary injury evidence
sections.cue: Both rulings and the dismissal stand
paragraphs: Rule 42(b) allowed separate trials for convenience, economy, expedition, or avoidance of prejudice while preserving a jury determination. Product identity could dispose of the entire case against Aquaslide. Several days of severe-injury and damages testimony would add nothing if Aquaslide did not make the slide and could prejudice consideration of that defense.

The Beecks retained a jury trial on identity, and its unchallenged finding achieved the contemplated economy. Finding no abuse of discretion in either ruling, the Eighth Circuit affirmed the judgment. It did not hold the slide safe, find no one responsible, or foreclose every possible claim against another party.
